The vertical shear instability (VSI) acts as a hydrodynamic mechanism in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, effectively transporting angular momentum from the gas to drive disk evolution and potentially triggering planet formation. We further demonstrate that turbulence varies significantly depending on dust radius, with smaller particles remaining more actively involved in dynamics than larger ones. These outcomes highlight the necessity of incorporating realistic dust physics when modeling disk turbulence and chemical/physical development.

Precise magnetic field measurements are crucial for advancing fundamental physics, geophysics, and material science. Although techniques like NMR, NL-MOS, and first-order magnetometry rely heavily on nuclear magnetic moments to detect these changes, this paper introduces a new method utilizing atomic interferometry that sidesteps such constraints. The proposed approach detects minute magnetic field variations by observing shifts in the local magnetic flux penetrating a superconductor, measured via atomic interferometry. Specifically, a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) magnetic wire modulates a cold atomic beam of rubidium-87 atoms; as the local field changes induced by a test sample alter the flux through the YIG's superconducting core (driven by the Meissner effect), an atomic interferometric phase shift occurs. This phase shift allows for the precise detection of local field changes ($\Delta B$) as small as ~20 nT at a 1 $\mu$m distance from the sample, achieved with an average measurement time of 20 minutes. The sensitivity corresponds to a magnetic field gradient of ~1 $\mu$T cm$^{-1}$ or a gradient product of ~0.2 nT $\mu$m, with the detection limit primarily constrained by the spatial resolution of the atomic beam.

The increasing prevalence of skin cancer has spurred greater interest in diagnosing it effectively. While deep learning excels at classification, the presence of outlier samples in datasets can significantly hinder model performance, a problem known as domain shift. Although various approaches exist for handling outliers in image classification, there is currently no method that specifically addresses this issue in dermatological image analysis. Consequently, the present study proposes an approach designed to mitigate the adverse effects of outliers during skin cancer classification. This method integrates a convolutional neural network (CNN) with outlier detection techniques, utilizing entropy to distinguish and correct anomalies within the training data. Evaluated against public dermatological datasets, the proposed entropic and neural network-based method achieves superior results compared to standard models trained on outlier-containing data. Notably, the study's framework detects domain shift problems, offering a practical solution for enhancing skin cancer diagnostic accuracy when dealing with diverse image sources.

We examine the internal coherence of electroweak symmetry breaking, alongside phenomenological frameworks for neutrinos and dark matter, within the context of the Minimal Simplex Model. This extension of the Standard Model incorporates a single additional scalar singlet and aligns with the Minimal Simplex Model, also recognized as the Minimal Scoto-See-Saw Model. Distinct from both the Type-I and Type-See neutrino seesaw mechanisms, our combined approach utilizes type-I seesaw techniques during high-energy physics regimes and type-II seesaw methods at low energies.
